newsitem.title: PANAMA: International flights partially resume in Panama.
newsitem.headline: International flights partially resume in Panama.

text.p: Traffic at Panama's Tocumen International Airport partially resumed on Wednesday after Panamanian authorities replaced striking air traffic controllers with workers from the United States.
National carrier COPA resumed international service but foreign airlines were still not flying into the airport, which normally handles about 200 flights a day.
"We have adopted a contingency plan for backlogged international flights scheduled to arrive later today," Civil Air Service spokesman Victor de la Hoz said.

At least 49 of 94 striking air traffic controllers were dismissed after they stopped work demanding better pay and pension benefits. De la Hoz said the contingency measures would allow airport authorities to stagger workers brought in from the U.S. during international traffic peak hours.

He said four air traffic controllers from the American company Westinghouse had already arrived. "They will be operating the radar. They know the Panama radar system very well," he said. A local subsidiary of Westinghouse sold Panama its radar system.

Westinghouse workers will train new air traffic controllers, a process De la Hoz said could take at least a year. Panama's air traffic controllers' association criticised the replacement of the fired workers.

"It's absurd and damaging Panama's image. It shows Panamanians that if you go on strike you will be replaced by gringos," Claudio Dutary, the association's vice-president and one of the dismissed air traffic controllers, told Reuters.
A Continental Airlines official said U.S. carriers were not flying into Tocumen to avoid any risks to passengers.

"No American carrier is flying into Tocumen right now ... Small planes are flying, but by sight. The situation is too dangerous for passengers. We hope to resume operations tomorrow," the official said.

The controllers walked out after talks with the government on a pay hike to $2,000 a month from an average of $600 broke down last weekend. They also want a package allowing them to retire earlier than the national average of 62 years for men and 57 years for women.
